URL: https://www.iranintl.com/en/202610146688
(Iran International, 00:57 BST 14 Oct)

The confrontation stems from a September 27 security incident near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, southwest England. Five British men were initially arrested after three suspicious vans were stopped near the base. Police found gasoline in the vehicles but no explosives.

Two more men, including a dual British-Iranian national, were subsequently arrested. All seven have been released on bail.

US officials told Reuters that the suspected plot involved a possible Iranian drone attack. Trump later said a threat linked to Iran prompted Washington to withdraw its B-1 bombers from Fairford, adding that the United States knew who had made the threat.

The Trump administration believes the Iranian threats were intended to kill US personnel and destroy American aircraft, AP reported Tuesday, citing a US official. British officials have not confirmed that assessment, and it remains unclear whether those arrested near Fairford were connected to the alleged drone threat.

RAF Fairford has been used by US bombers involved in strikes against Iran. Tehran has previously said bases used to attack its territory could be considered legitimate targets.

Fairford fuels Iran-UK confrontation

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday the suspected plot was “highly likely” coordinated in Iran and “almost certainly” directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said investigators believed an individual based in Iran was behind the incident.

Britain summoned Iran's ambassador and sanctioned two Iranian nationals over alleged involvement in hostile operations abroad.

Tehran responded Tuesday by summoning British Ambassador Hugo Shorter. Iranian Foreign Ministry official Alireza Yousefi rejected the accusations, demanded evidence and warned that Tehran would “seriously reconsider” bilateral relations if Britain failed to substantiate its claims.

The diplomatic confrontation came as MI5 Director General Ken McCallum warned Tuesday that Iran was increasingly turning its attention to military sites and other “harder targets” in Britain.

McCallum said the Fairford incident was “not unique” and that more than 50 people had been arrested in Iran-linked operations in Britain over the previous 12 months. He said Iranian activity had increasingly extended beyond traditional targets such as opponents of Tehran to Jewish sites and military installations.

Britain, the United States and 27 other countries also backed London's attribution of Iranian involvement in the Fairford incident, saying it followed a broader pattern of alleged Iranian attacks and hostile activity abroad.

Iran has denied involvement in the Fairford incident and rejected British accusations of directing hostile operations in the country.

"])•••$RC("B:5","S:5")More StoriesUK blames IRGC for RAF plot, vows crackdown on Iranian networksOct 12, 2026, 17:28 GMT+1Listen to this article100%A B-1 bomber takes off from RAF Fairford airbase, as the US removes its B-1 bombers one week after several men were arrested on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act, in this screengrab obtained from a social media video in Fairford, Gloucestershire, Britain October 4, 2026.Britain said on Monday that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had “almost certainly” directed a suspected plot targeting RAF Fairford, as it vowed to crack down on Iranian criminal networks, sanctioned two Iranian nationals and summoned Iran’s ambassador.

RAF Fairford in southwest England, which had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, became the focus of a major security operation after five British men were arrested nearby in the early hours of Sept. 27 on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offences.

US officials have said the suspected plot involved a drone attack. President Donald Trump said last week that an Iran-linked threat had prompted the United States to withdraw its bombers from the base.

“I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard,” Prime Minister Andy Burnham told parliament.

Iran has denied involvement. Iran’s ambassador to Britain, Seyed Ali Mousavi, on Monday rejected any Iranian role in the suspected plot and said Tehran was willing to cooperate with British authorities investigating the incident, state news agency IRNA reported.

Details of the suspected plot remain limited. The five British men were later released on police bail under what authorities described as stringent conditions. Two other arrested men, including a British-Iranian national, were also released.

Police said petrol was found in vans seized during the investigation but no viable explosive was discovered.

“We will not tolerate these threats on our soil,” Burnham said. “We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm.”

Sanctions and diplomatic summons

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he had instructed his department to summon Iran’s ambassador.

“Iran’s continued attempts to undermine the security of the United Kingdom and international partners through its criminal networks, proxy groups and state-backed malign activity is unacceptable,” Miliband said.

Britain also sanctioned Ruhollah Bazghandi and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki under its Iran sanctions regime.

The UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said Bazghandi, whom it identified as the IRGC’s head of counterespionage operations, was suspected of planning or conducting espionage for Iran and of involvement in threatening, planning or conducting attacks against people and assets in Britain or other countries.

Jakki was sanctioned for allegedly supporting or assisting activity involving threats, plans or attacks against people outside Iran. Britain described him as a facilitator for the already sanctioned Zindashti criminal network, which it says has been involved in plots targeting Iranian dissidents.

Foreign ministries from nearly 30 countries, including the United States, Canada, France and Germany, issued a joint statement condemning “Iran’s use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners.”

“The UK has also concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors,” the statement said.

British authorities have for years accused Iran of involvement in plots and attempted assassinations in Britain using criminal networks and proxies, allegations Tehran has repeatedly denied. Britain said last year that it had identified 20 credible Iran-backed threats to kill or kidnap people based in the UK.

In July, Britain used new state-threat powers to ban support for the IRGC and Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, or HAYI, a linked group that had claimed responsibility for seven attacks earlier this year targeting sites connected to Jewish and Israeli communities and Persian-language media.

Listen to this article100%File photo: The inaugural double-stack container train linking Iran and China, July 2024Washington’s new sanctions are unlikely to stop a China–Iran freight train at the border, but may make the route Tehran has turned to under pressure from the US naval blockade costlier and less reliable.

The blockade has sharply restricted maritime trade, while years of sanctions have squeezed Iran’s access to international finance. But not every trade channel had already closed.

Trains carrying goods from China were still reaching Iran before the latest US measures. The question now is whether sanctions on Iran’s railway companies will narrow that remaining route and complicate the flow of goods, including auto parts, carried on it.

Last week, the US Treasury designated three Iranian rail companies: the state-owned Islamic Republic of Iran Railway Company, known as RAI; Raja Passenger Trains Company; and private freight operator Railway Transportation Company.

The department said Iran had turned to rail to sustain trade and transport oil as the maritime blockade took hold.

The sanctions block the US-based property of the designated companies and prohibit US persons from dealing with them, while separate sectoral determinations give Washington wider scope to impose future designations. They do not automatically block every foreign railway, freight company or shipment connected to Iran.

The more immediate effect may be caution among companies involved in the trade. Banks may reject payments. Insurers and equipment suppliers may refuse to handle business involving designated companies. Others may charge higher fees or take longer to process shipments.

None of this would close the railway, but together it could make the route less dependable.

A useful route, with clear limits

The China–Iran rail connection is no longer just a proposal. In September, a block train bound for Iran was reported traveling through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan before entering at Sarakhs.

A train from Xi’an to Iran’s Aprin dry port in 2025 was reported to have taken about 15 days, compared with an estimated 30 to 40 days by sea. Iranian railway officials also reported that 43 freight trains arrived from China in the first nine months of 2025.

Those figures show a route in use, although they do not indicate how much of Iran’s overall trade moves by rail.

Rail can move selected goods, industrial inputs, equipment and containerized cargo faster than shipping by sea. But it cannot replace the volume carried by tankers or bulk freighters.

Treasury says Iran is using rail to help transport oil, but its announcement provides no figures for oil moved this way. There is therefore little evidence that rail is a meaningful substitute for seaborne oil exports.
